interactive.title: Your DOL starter, live
interactive.whatAmILookingAt:
A DOL starter, drawn with its parts numbered 1 to 10. The supply (1) comes in on L1, L2, L3 and N, through fuses or a breaker and the four-pole isolator (2). The three main contacts (5) feed the motor (6) through the overload's heaters (9), one in each line. The coil circuit runs from L3 through Stop (8), then Start (3) with the latching contact (7) across it, then the coil (4) and the overload's contact (10), to the neutral. Dashed lines join the parts that work together: the coil with 5 and 7, and the heaters with 10.

In the live picture the fed parts light up, and the coil glows while it is fed. A meter shows the current in one line. A bar beside the heaters fills as the overload warms. When it is full, 10 opens and the motor stops.
interactive.ignores: The picture runs on a sped-up clock. The run-up, the overload heating and the cooling take far longer in real life. The start surge of 7 times is one example from a range. The motor current slider sets the current directly, as if the load grew. The supply cut is long enough for the coil to let go. A contactor may ride through a very short dip. That depends on the contactor. The picture does not show a short circuit, only the fuses or breaker that would clear one. The control circuit is drawn fed from one phase and the neutral. Many starters feed a 400 V coil across two lines instead. Only the motor current slider heats the overload. The start surge does not, so repeated starts never trip it here.

explain.text:
A DOL starter switches a motor straight onto the full supply through a contactor. Start pulls the contactor in. A contact across Start then keeps the coil fed, so the motor runs on after you let go. Anything that opens the coil's circuit drops it all out. It stays out until someone presses Start again.

Follow the coil circuit in the drawing. Start (3), Stop (8) and the overload's release contact (10) are all in series with the coil (4). Assume it is fed from one phase and the neutral, so it sees 230 V. Start is normally open and sprung. Press it and the coil is fed. The coil's magnet pulls the contactor's moving part in. That closes the three main contacts (5), and the motor starts on full voltage. The same movement closes a small extra contact, the [[latching contact]] (7). It is wired across Start. So when Start springs back, the coil still has a path through 7. The coil does the pulling and the holding. The latching contact only keeps the coil fed.

Stop is normally closed. Press it and the coil circuit opens. The coil lets go, so the main contacts and 7 open together. Let go of Stop and nothing happens, because Start and 7 are both open now. The overload works the same way. Too much current heats its bimetal strips (9) until they bend and open 10. The overload has no main contacts of its own. It stops the motor only by opening the coil's circuit. So does a supply cut long enough to drop the coil out. When the supply comes back, Start and 7 are still open, so the motor stays stopped. That is [[no-volt protection]]. A machine does not start up again by itself after a power cut. A pump run by a float or pressure switch is different. That switch stays made, so the pump restarts by itself when the supply returns.[^13]

**A contactor with a latching contact across Start gives no-volt protection. Stop, the overload or a power cut can open its coil circuit. After that, only Start makes it again.**

analogy.text: Think of a fire door held open by a magnet. While the magnet is fed, the door stays open. If the fire alarm or a power cut cuts its supply, the door swings shut. When the power returns, the door stays shut. Someone has to push it open again, just as someone has to press Start.
analogy.breaks: The magnet's supply does not pass through the door. The starter's coil is fed through its own latching contact. So once the coil lets go, it has cut its own feed. Only Start can feed it again.

practice.text:
- Isolate, lock off and prove dead before you open a starter. Prove all three lines and the neutral dead, with a tester you prove before and after.
- Read the coil's voltage on its label and check how it is wired. On a 400 V supply, a 230 V coil needs a phase and the neutral. A 400 V coil goes across two lines.
- Set the overload to the motor's full-load current from its nameplate. Do not set it to a trip current.
- Make sure fuses or a breaker ahead of it give the short-circuit protection. The overload does not.
- Check Start and Stop both work before you hand it back.

**Rule of thumb:** if the motor runs only while Start is held, look at the latching contact (7) first.

**Worked example:** start the showroom motor DOL. It is 11 kW and 23.08 A at full load. Set the overload to 23.08 A. It should hold at 1.05 × 23.08 = 24.23 A and trip slowly, on its trip curve, at 1.2 × 23.08 = 27.70 A.[^4] While it runs up, the motor usually draws 6 × 23.08 = 138 A to 8 × 23.08 = 185 A. The contactor makes that current every start. Star-delta would cut it to 138 ÷ 3 = 46 A to 185 ÷ 3 = 62 A.

**Common mistakes**
- Thinking the latching contact holds the main contacts in. The coil holds them. The latch only keeps the coil fed.
- Expecting the motor to restart after a power cut. It stays stopped until Start is pressed.
- Trusting the overload to clear a short circuit. That is the fuses' or breaker's job.
- Fitting a coil for the wrong voltage. Too high a voltage can burn it out. Too low, and it may not pull in.
- Taking a dropped-out contactor as dead. Its supply side can still be live.

summary.title: The DOL starter
summary.for: Starting a cage motor straight on the full supply. Start pulls the contactor in. The latching contact keeps its coil fed. Anything that opens the coil circuit drops it out until Start is pressed again.
summary.rule:
Start (3) N/O, with the latching contact (7) across it.
Stop (8) N/C and the overload's contact (10) in series with the coil (4).
Extra Stops go in series, extra Starts in parallel with Start.
Coil voltage must match its wiring: 230 V phase to neutral, 400 V across two lines.

DOL start: usually 6 to 8 × full-load current, sometimes over 10.
Overload set to full-load current: holds at 1.05 ×, trips slowly at 1.2 × on its trip curve.
Star-delta: about a third of the current, about a quarter of the torque.

Runs only while Start is held: check 7. Will not start: check the overload first.

traps.text: The coil pulls and holds the main contacts. The latching contact only keeps the coil fed once Start springs back.
traps.cite: [^14] [^15] DOL study sheet; Basic Motor Control

traps.text: After a power cut the motor stays stopped until someone presses Start. That is no-volt protection.
The overload does not clear a short circuit. Fuses or a breaker do.
Set the overload to the motor's full-load current, not a trip current.
Isolate, lock off and prove dead first. A contactor can hold line voltage with its coil off.

applied.problem: Four overstatements: the 1 s supply cut is not labelled an example where it appears; a contactor breaks more than running current if opened mid-start; a dropped-out contactor is live only while not isolated; worn contacts as THE commonest cause of single phasing is one maker’s claim.

The 230 V phase-to-neutral rule holds only on a 400/230 V supply (not, say, a 440 V ship supply with no neutral); “for a moment” understates a run-up that can last seconds; the supply side of a dropped-out contactor is live only until isolated.
The coil rule ‘230 V phase to neutral, 400 V across two lines’ is true only on a 400 V supply; on the card alone it reads as universal, and Dan will meet 440 V ship supplies.
